To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) PDP models can learn to recall novel words, (2) PDP models learn to recall novel items by generalizing over similar words, (3) generalization is supported by selective coding, (4) selective coding is achieved by co-activating items in STM.

PDP models of immediate recall can learn localist codes in the presence of noise, that this is possible when the models generalize to novel stimuli, and that these conditions may explain selective coding observed in cortex.

(1) recurrent PDP models of STM can learn localist codes when the model can generalize; (2) the model's capacity for generalization depends on the model's capacity to co-activate items in short-term-memory; (3) the model's ability to co-activate information depends on the model being able to learn selective codes in a highly distributed manner; and (4) the model learns selective codes when it is able to learn in an unsupervised manner.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how the brain learns to recognize objects, words, faces and other stimuli.
the conditions under which neural networks can learn to represent information in a highly distributed or selective manner.
the conditions that lead to the emergence of localist codes in PDP models of STM and learning, and the implications of these results for the study of neural coding in the brain.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the brain uses localist codes when generalization and fast learning are needed, and distributed codes when fast learning is not required and generalization is not needed.
selective codes exist in the brain, but they are not the result of the brain trying to avoid catastrophic interference, but of the brain trying hard to learn generalizations.
both fast learning and STM are important to understand the emergence of selective coding in hippocampal and cortical networks.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the selective coding of information is a consequence of the interplay between the demands for fast learning, generalization, and STM.
“selective codes in cortex may be a byproduct of generalization and STM”.
selective coding is not a necessary consequence of the brain's architecture, but a consequence of the brain having to perform multiple tasks.
The main takeaway from our work is that
selective coding is not an all or none phenomenon, but rather it depends on the learning task, the type of learning, and the architecture of the model.
we need to take into account the interaction between the different cognitive functions supported by the brain in order to understand how neural codes are formed.
the existence of selective neural codes is not necessarily incompatible with the existence of distributed neural codes.
